# Cognitive Biases vs Cognitive Distortions: What's the Difference?

> Cognitive biases come from judgment and decision-making research. Cognitive distortions come from CBT. How they differ, where they overlap, and which ten thinking patterns are most worth working on in everyday life.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-biases-vs-distortions.html
- Published: 2026-10-21
- Updated: 2026-11-03
- Reading time: 6 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** Cognitive biases are systematic errors in judgment studied in decision-making research (Kahneman and Tversky). Cognitive distortions are exaggerated thinking patterns that fuel painful emotions, catalogued in CBT (Beck). The lists overlap. For everyday life, start with negativity bias, confirmation bias, catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation and social comparison.

## The short answer

A **cognitive bias** is a systematic error in judgment that affects everyone, like anchoring on the first price you see. A **cognitive distortion** is an exaggerated pattern of thinking, like assuming the worst, that tends to fuel painful emotions. Biases come from judgment and decision-making research. Distortions come from cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). The two lists overlap, but they aren't the same list.

## Two traditions, two purposes

Biases were mapped by researchers like Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky from the 1970s onward. They asked how people make judgments under uncertainty and found predictable errors: anchoring, availability, overconfidence. The point was to describe how minds work, not to treat anyone.

Distortions were named by Aaron Beck and later clinicians working with depression and anxiety. They noticed that distressed people's thoughts followed recognisable shapes, such as catastrophising, mind reading and all-or-nothing thinking, and that those shapes could be caught and tested. The APA describes cognitive therapy as helping people identify problematic thoughts and weigh them against evidence. Distortions are the labels that make that work possible.

So a bias can be socially important, driving polarisation or bad investments, without being the most useful thing to work on in your own head at 11pm. The [12 biases shaping 2026](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-biases-2026.html) are ranked for their effect on society. The list below is ranked for usefulness in everyday thoughts.

## Ten patterns, ranked for everyday use

*Thinking patterns, an everyday example of each, and where to start*

| Thinking pattern | What it looks like | Where to start |
|---|---|---|
| Negativity bias | Fixating on one criticism | Start here |
| Confirmation bias | Looking for proof that nobody likes you | Start here |
| Catastrophising | Assuming a setback means everything will fail | Start here |
| Mind reading | Assuming someone is judging you | Start here |
| All-or-nothing thinking | Believing anything short of perfect is failure | Start here |
| Overgeneralisation | One rejection means nobody will accept you | Start here |
| Social comparison | Feeling behind everyone else | Start here |
| Sunk cost fallacy | Staying in an unhealthy commitment | Next |
| Availability bias | Assuming bad experiences are universal | Next |
| Fundamental attribution error | Reading others' actions as personal attacks | Next |

Catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking and overgeneralisation aren't on the societal list at all. That's deliberate. They're among the most commonly taught distortions in CBT because they show up in the thoughts behind a bad day far more often than anchoring does.

## Where the lists overlap

Some biases do the same work as a distortion:

- **Confirmation bias and mental filter.** Once you believe you're unlikable, you notice every cold reply and forget the warm ones.
- **Negativity bias and discounting the positive.** One insult outweighs a hundred kind comments, and the kind ones "don't count".
- **Availability bias and overgeneralisation.** A few vivid examples become "this always happens".
- **Fundamental attribution error and labelling.** One late reply becomes "they're rude", a verdict on a person, not a reading of a situation.

These are the biases worth practising on personally: they feed straight into how you feel about yourself and other people.

## Learn the pattern before the name

You don't need the vocabulary to use the method. "Am I assuming the worst?" is easier to answer in the moment than "Is this catastrophising?" The terms are useful later, once you've recognised the pattern in your own thoughts a few times and want a short handle for it. The aim is to notice the pattern while it's running, not to memorise a glossary.

[Five thinking patterns to catch first](https://behaviorized.net/articles/five-thinking-patterns.html) gives a plain question for each of the most common ones. The full CBT list, with examples, is in [the 10 cognitive distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html).

## Questions people ask

### Is confirmation bias a cognitive distortion?

Not formally, since it comes from decision-making research. But it works like the CBT distortion called mental filter, which is why it's worth catching in your own thoughts.

### Are cognitive distortions a sign of a mental health condition?

No. Everyone uses them. They become a problem when they're frequent, rigid and drive distress, which is when CBT, self-guided or with a therapist, can help.

### What does CBT do about them?

It helps you identify the thought, test it against evidence, and replace it with a more accurate one. The target is accuracy, not positivity. [The thought record](https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html) is the standard way to do it.

## A note on limits

This is general education drawn from CBT, not a diagnosis or treatment. If your thoughts are tied to persistent low mood, anxiety or distress, or are getting worse, a mental health professional can help. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.

## Sources

- American Psychological Association. Cognitive therapy. *APA Dictionary of Psychology*. [dictionary.apa.org](https://dictionary.apa.org/cognitive-therapy)
- Beck, A. T., Rush, A. J., Shaw, B. F., & Emery, G. (1979). *Cognitive Therapy of Depression*. Guilford Press.
- Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. *Science*, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
- Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, Fast and Slow*. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

# Five Thinking Patterns to Catch First

> Catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, confirmation bias and overgeneralisation: the five thinking patterns worth catching first, each with a plain question that tests it and a worked example.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/five-thinking-patterns.html
- Published: 2026-10-21
- Updated: 2026-11-03
- Reading time: 6 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** Five thinking patterns drive a large share of everyday distress: catastrophising, mind reading, all-or-nothing thinking, confirmation bias and overgeneralisation. Each can be tested with one plain question, such as "Are you assuming the worst?" Learn to spot the pattern first; the psychological term can come later.

There are dozens of named cognitive biases and distortions. You don't need them all. These five are common, they drive a large share of everyday distress, and each one can be tested with a single plain question you can ask yourself in the moment.

Each pattern below starts with the question you'd actually ask, not the term. "Are you assuming the worst?" is easier to answer at 11pm than "Is this catastrophising?" The names are there for later, once you've spotted the pattern in your own head a few times.

## 1. Are you assuming the worst?

**The pattern:** catastrophising, treating a setback as proof that everything will fail.

> **Thought:** "I missed the deadline. I'm going to lose this job."

**The question:** What's the worst outcome you're predicting, and how likely is it?

> **Reframe:** "Worst case is a hard conversation with my manager. Losing the job over one late deliverable is unlikely, and I've hit every other deadline this quarter."

Making the prediction specific is most of the work. A vague dread can't be tested; "I'll be fired by Friday" can.

## 2. Do you actually know what they think?

**The pattern:** mind reading, assuming someone is judging you without them saying so.

> **Thought:** "She went quiet after my joke. She thinks I'm an idiot."

**The question:** What evidence do you have about what this person thinks?

> **Reframe:** "All I saw was a pause. She could have been distracted, tired, or thinking about something else. I don't know, and I could ask."

## 3. Is there anything between perfect and failure?

**The pattern:** all-or-nothing thinking, believing anything short of perfect counts as failure.

> **Thought:** "I skipped the gym twice this week. I've blown it."

**The question:** Is there a possibility between complete success and complete failure?

> **Reframe:** "Three sessions out of five is most of a week. It's more than I managed last month."

## 4. What are you leaving out?

**The pattern:** confirmation bias, collecting proof for what you already believe and dropping the rest.

> **Thought:** "Nobody replied to my message in the group chat. Nobody here likes me."

**The question:** What evidence might you be overlooking?

> **Reframe:** "Two of them invited me out last week, and the chat's been quiet all day for everyone."

This one comes from decision-making research rather than CBT, but in personal life it behaves like a distortion: it keeps a painful belief alive by filtering what you notice. More on that in [cognitive biases vs cognitive distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-biases-vs-distortions.html).

## 5. Is this one event, or really a pattern?

**The pattern:** overgeneralisation, turning one experience into a rule about your life.

> **Thought:** "I got rejected for this role. Nobody's ever going to hire me."

**The question:** Does this one experience establish a pattern?

> **Reframe:** "One rejection from one company. I've been hired before, and I've applied to four places so far, not forty."

Watch for the words "always", "never", "nobody" and "everyone". They're usually the sign that one data point has become a law.

## How to practise

1. **Catch the thought.** Write it down in the words it used, as soon as you notice a shift in mood.
2. **Ask the question.** Pick whichever of the five fits. Often two do.
3. **Write what the evidence supports.** Not the opposite of the thought, and not a pep talk. The version a fair witness would agree with.

The aim isn't to memorise terms. It's to recognise the patterns working in your own thoughts quickly enough to question them. [The CBT thought record](https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html) turns these three steps into a full exercise, and [the 10 cognitive distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html) covers the rest of the CBT list once these five feel familiar.

## Questions people ask

### Why these five?

They're common, they feed straight into everyday distress, and each can be tested with one question. Four are among the distortions most often taught in CBT; confirmation bias is the decision-making bias that does the most similar work.

### Do I need to know the psychological terms?

No. The plain question works better in the moment. Terms become a useful shorthand later.

### What if the thought is true?

Sometimes it partly is. The questions aren't meant to argue you out of reality. They separate what happened from the story layered on top, so you can deal with the part that's real.

## A note on limits

These questions are self-help drawn from CBT, not a treatment on their own. If your thoughts are tied to persistent low mood, anxiety or distress, or are getting worse, work with a mental health professional. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.

## Sources

- American Psychological Association. Cognitive therapy. *APA Dictionary of Psychology*. [dictionary.apa.org](https://dictionary.apa.org/cognitive-therapy)
- Beck, A. T., Rush, A. J., Shaw, B. F., & Emery, G. (1979). *Cognitive Therapy of Depression*. Guilford Press.
- Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, Fast and Slow*. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

Everything stays on your device. [Download Reframed on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/reframed-rewire-your-thoughts/id6768231681)

# Psycho-Cybernetics and CBT: How to Actually Change Your Self-Image

> What Maxwell Maltz's Psycho-Cybernetics gets right about self-image, how it maps onto cognitive behavioural therapy, what the evidence says about changing your mindset, and the daily practice that does the changing.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/psycho-cybernetics-and-cbt.html
- Published: 2026-10-20
- Updated: 2026-11-20
- Reading time: 8 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** Maxwell Maltz argued that behaviour follows self-image. CBT agrees, and supplies the method: a self-image is held up by many small automatic thoughts, so you change it by catching, testing and rewriting those thoughts one at a time. Change takes repetition. The "21 days" figure is a myth; one study found new habits took 66 days on average.

If you've read *Psycho-Cybernetics*, you already have the most important idea in this article: you don't act on reality, you act on your picture of yourself in it. Change the picture and the behaviour follows.

What the book doesn't give you is a reliable way to change the picture. This article connects Maltz's ideas to cognitive behavioural therapy, the approach with decades of trials behind it, and shows where the two meet in a practice you can do today.

## What is Psycho-Cybernetics?

**Psycho-Cybernetics is a 1960 self-help book by Maxwell Maltz, a plastic surgeon.** Its core claim is that your self-image, your settled sense of who you are, sets the limits of what you will attempt and achieve. Maltz described the mind as a goal-seeking system that steers towards whatever target that self-image gives it.

Maltz came to this through his patients. Some had their appearance changed and their lives transformed. Others had the same surgery and felt no different, because the picture they carried of themselves hadn't moved. He concluded that the inner image was doing the real work.

He borrowed the word "cybernetics" from Norbert Wiener's science of feedback systems. A guided missile senses where it is, compares that to the target, and corrects course. Maltz argued the mind works the same way: give it a target and it will steer, using feedback from each attempt. Give it a target set by a poor self-image and it will steer just as efficiently towards failure.

## How does Psycho-Cybernetics relate to CBT?

**They describe the same loop from two directions.** What Maltz called the self-image, CBT calls core beliefs: deep, general statements like "I'm not capable" or "people leave". What Maltz called the feedback mechanism, CBT breaks into steps: a situation triggers an automatic thought, the thought produces a feeling, the feeling drives behaviour, and the behaviour produces evidence that seems to confirm the belief.

> **Core belief:** "I don't finish things."

> **Automatic thought:** "This project will go the way the others did."

The thought makes starting feel pointless, so you start late, so the project goes badly, so the belief gets another piece of evidence. Maltz would call that a servo-mechanism aimed at the wrong target. CBT calls it a maintenance cycle. On our home page we draw it as [the loop](https://behaviorized.net/index.html#the-loop).

The difference is in the fix. Maltz leaned on visualisation: rehearse the new self in your imagination until it feels real. CBT goes after the beliefs themselves, one thought at a time, by checking them against the evidence. The roots of that approach are old. Aaron Beck, who founded cognitive therapy, wrote in his 1979 treatment manual that its philosophical origins can be traced back to the Stoic philosophers, who taught that we're disturbed less by events than by our judgements of them.

## Can you actually change your mindset?

**Yes, but more slowly and more specifically than most mindset books suggest.** The strongest evidence is for CBT. A 2012 review by Hofmann and colleagues looked across more than a hundred meta-analyses and found strong support for CBT, particularly for anxiety, stress and anger problems. The method changes beliefs by working on the thoughts that express them.

Two popular claims hold up less well:

- **"21 days to change."** Maltz observed that his patients needed a minimum of about three weeks to adjust to a changed face, and suggested a similar minimum for a new self-image. Retellings dropped "minimum" and turned it into a rule. When researchers at University College London tracked people building a new daily habit (Lally et al., 2009), the average time to automaticity was 66 days, with very wide variation between people.
- **"Adopt a growth mindset and your results change."** Carol Dweck's idea that abilities can be developed is sound and useful. But a 2018 pair of meta-analyses (Sisk et al., *Psychological Science*) found that the overall effects of mindset interventions on achievement were weak, with larger benefits mainly for students at academic risk. Believing you can change helps. It is not the change.

The pattern across all of this is the same. Insight sets the direction. Repetition does the moving.

## From insight to reps

Most people who read *Psycho-Cybernetics*, *Mindset* or *Atomic Habits* come away agreeing with them. Then the old self-image carries on running, because agreeing with a book doesn't touch the sentence your brain produces at 2am.

The self-image isn't stored as a picture you can repaint in one session. It's held up by hundreds of small, specific, automatic thoughts, each one a tiny vote for the old verdict. The way to change the verdict is to change the votes, one at a time:

- **Catch the thought.** The exact sentence, in its exact words: "I always freeze when it matters."
- **Name the pattern.** "Always" is overgeneralisation. See [the ten cognitive distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html).
- **Test it.** Evidence for, evidence against. The [thought record](https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html) is the formal version.
- **Write the accurate version.** Not the inspiring one. The one a fair witness would sign.

> **Old vote:** "I always freeze when it matters."

> **New vote:** "I froze in Tuesday's meeting. I didn't freeze in the two before it, or on the call with the client."

This is where Maltz's mental rehearsal and CBT meet. Writing the accurate version is a rehearsal too, but it's one your brain can't refute, because every word of it is checkable. That's also why [affirmations often backfire](https://behaviorized.net/articles/affirmations-vs-reframing.html): a new self-image declared without evidence starts an argument the old one wins.

## If you're into mindset work

Read the books. They're good at the part they're for: convincing you that the self-image is real, that it drives behaviour, and that it can change. Here's how they map onto the practice:

- **Maltz, *Psycho-Cybernetics*:** the self-image as a target. In CBT terms, the core belief you're working on.
- **Dweck, *Mindset*:** the belief that ability can grow. A useful core belief to build, by collecting evidence for it.
- **Clear, *Atomic Habits*:** every action is a vote for the person you want to become. A reframed thought is a vote too.
- **The Stoics:** it's the judgement, not the event. The idea CBT was built on.

What all four leave to you is the daily practice. That's the part worth building a habit around. If you're choosing a tool for it, [CBT tools compared](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cbt-tools-compared.html) breaks down how workbooks, thought diaries, chatbots and Reframed fit different jobs.

## Questions people ask

### Does Psycho-Cybernetics work?

Its central idea, that the way you see yourself limits what you attempt, lines up with how CBT understands core beliefs, and CBT has a strong research base. The book's specific methods, like its visualisation exercises and the 21-day figure, were never tested the way CBT has been. Treat it as a useful frame, and use a tested method to do the changing.

### Is Psycho-Cybernetics the same as CBT?

No. Psycho-Cybernetics is a 1960 self-help book by a plastic surgeon. CBT is a clinical approach developed by Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis in the 1960s and tested in hundreds of trials. They share one idea: the beliefs you hold about yourself shape what you feel and do, and those beliefs can be changed.

### Does it really take 21 days to change?

No. Twenty-one days was Maltz's observed minimum for patients adjusting to a changed appearance. The best-known study of habit formation found an average of 66 days for a new daily habit to become automatic, and some people took far longer.

### How do you change your self-image?

Not by declaring a new one. Catch the specific thought that expresses the old self-image, name the pattern behind it, test it against evidence, and write the version that survives. Repeated daily, those accurate versions build a record the old belief can't argue with.

### Is a growth mindset the same as a positive self-image?

Not quite. A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can be developed. Self-image is the broader picture of who you are. Both are beliefs, so both respond to the same method: notice the thought, check it, and replace it with a more accurate one, again and again.

## A note on limits

Everything here is self-help drawn from CBT, not a treatment in itself. Psycho-Cybernetics and the other books mentioned are popular works, not clinical guidance. If your self-image is tied to depression, trauma or long-standing low self-esteem, or your mood is getting worse, work with a professional. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.

## Sources

- Maltz, M. (1960). *Psycho-Cybernetics*. Prentice-Hall.
- Beck, A. T., Rush, A. J., Shaw, B. F., & Emery, G. (1979). *Cognitive Therapy of Depression*. Guilford Press.
- Hofmann, S. G., Asnaani, A., Vonk, I. J. J., Sawyer, A. T., & Fang, A. (2012). The efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy: A review of meta-analyses. *Cognitive Therapy and Research*, 36(5), 427–440. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3584580/)
- Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. *European Journal of Social Psychology*, 40(6), 998–1009. [UCL summary](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2009/aug/how-long-does-it-take-form-habit)
- Sisk, V. F., Burgoyne, A. P., Sun, J., Butler, J. L., & Macnamara, B. N. (2018). To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses. *Psychological Science*, 29(4), 549–571.
- Wood, J. V., Perunovic, W. Q. E., & Lee, J. W. (2009). Positive self-statements: Power for some, peril for others. *Psychological Science*, 20(7), 860–866.

# The 10 Cognitive Distortions, With Examples

> A plain-language guide to the ten cognitive distortions used in CBT — all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising, mind reading and the rest — with real examples and the question that breaks each one.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html
- Published: 2026-08-19
- Updated: 2026-11-03
- Reading time: 8 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** Cognitive distortions are habits of thought that feel like facts. CBT names ten: all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation, mental filter, discounting the positive, jumping to conclusions, magnification and minimisation, emotional reasoning, "should" statements, labelling, and personalisation. Once you've named one, replace the thought with a more accurate version, not a more positive one.

A cognitive distortion is a habit of thought that feels like an observation. It arrives fully formed, in your own voice, with the weight of a fact — "I always ruin things" — and because it sounds like you, you rarely stop to check it.

Cognitive behavioural therapy's contribution was to notice that these habits come in a small number of recognisable shapes. Aaron Beck catalogued them in the 1960s while treating depression; David Burns popularised the list in *Feeling Good* (1980). Ten of them cover most of what your mind does to you on a bad day.

Naming the shape is most of the work. A thought you can label is a thought you can argue with.

## 1. All-or-nothing thinking

Also called black-and-white or polarised thinking. There are two boxes — success and failure — and no room between them. One missed run makes you someone who doesn't exercise. One awkward sentence makes the whole dinner a disaster.

> **The thought:** "I ate badly today, so the whole week is blown."

**The question that breaks it:** if this were a percentage instead of a verdict, what number would it be? Almost nothing in a life is 0 or 100.

## 2. Overgeneralisation

One event becomes a rule. The tell is the vocabulary: *always*, *never*, *everyone*, *nothing*. A single rejection stops being a thing that happened and becomes a description of how things go.

> **The thought:** "He didn't text back. I always get ghosted."

**The question:** how many times, exactly? Count. If the honest number is three out of fifteen, "always" is a lie you told yourself.

## 3. Mental filter

You pick out one negative detail and dwell on it until the whole picture darkens — like a drop of ink in a glass of water. Nine parts of the presentation landed. You are replaying the tenth.

> **The thought:** "She said one thing about the timeline. The review was a disaster."

**The question:** what else was in the room that I'm not counting?

## 4. Discounting the positive

The close relative of the mental filter, and meaner. Here the good things register — you just disqualify them. Praise was politeness. The win was luck. The effort doesn't count because it should have been easier.

> **The thought:** "They only said that to be nice."

**The question:** if a friend told me this about their own week, would I accept the same explanation?

## 5. Jumping to conclusions

Reading the situation without the data. It splits into two familiar moves:

### Mind reading

Deciding you know what someone thinks of you, and treating the guess as reported speech.

> **The thought:** "They think I'm not good enough for this."

### Fortune telling

Predicting the outcome, then reacting to the prediction as though it already happened.

> **The thought:** "There's no point applying. I won't get it."

**The question:** what would I need to see for this to be true — and have I seen it?

## 6. Magnification and minimisation

The volume knob. Your mistakes get turned up until they fill the room; your strengths get turned down until they're inaudible. Someone else's identical mistake, of course, gets handled at normal volume.

> **The thought:** "I sent a typo to the whole team. Everyone saw it. My degree was nothing special anyway."

**The question:** what weight would I give this if a colleague had done it?

## 7. Emotional reasoning

Treating a feeling as evidence. *I feel like a fraud, therefore I am one.* The logic is circular, but it's fast, and feelings are persuasive because they're happening inside you.

> **The thought:** "I feel useless today, so I must be failing at this."

**The question:** is this a fact about the world, or a fact about how I feel right now? Both can be real. Only one is evidence.

## 8. "Should" statements

A private rulebook nobody agreed to, enforced with guilt. Aimed inward it produces shame; aimed outward it produces resentment when other people fail to follow rules they never read.

> **The thought:** "I should be further along by now."

**The question:** who wrote this rule, and would I apply it to anyone else? Try swapping *should* for *I'd prefer to* and see whether the sentence survives.

## 9. Labelling

Overgeneralisation applied to a person instead of an event. You don't say "I made a mistake" — you say "I'm an idiot." The label converts a thing you did into a thing you are, which is much harder to change.

> **The thought:** "I'm a failure."

**The question:** what specifically happened? Describe the behaviour, not the person. "I missed the deadline" is workable. "I'm a failure" is not.

## 10. Personalisation and blame

Taking responsibility for events you didn't control — a partner's mood, a team's slipping deadline, someone else's bad day — or, in reverse, assigning all of it elsewhere and none of it to yourself.

> **The thought:** "The project's behind because of me."

**The question:** list every factor that contributed, then give each a share of the total. Your slice is usually real, and usually smaller than the one you assigned yourself.

## What to do once you've named one

Naming the distortion is step one, not the finish. The distorted thought loses its authority when you replace it with something more accurate — not more positive, more *accurate*.

> **Distorted:** "I ruined the presentation. Everyone noticed."

> **Balanced:** "I lost my place on slide four for about ten seconds. Two people asked follow-up questions afterwards, which they wouldn't have if it had been unwatchable."

Notice that the balanced version isn't cheerful. It doesn't claim the presentation was brilliant. It's just what a fair witness would have said — and a fair witness is exactly what a distorted thought lacks.

The formal version of this exercise is the thought record, and it's worth learning properly: [how to write a CBT thought record](https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html).

New to this? [Five thinking patterns to catch first](https://behaviorized.net/articles/five-thinking-patterns.html) narrows the list to a starting set, and [cognitive biases vs cognitive distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-biases-vs-distortions.html) explains how this CBT list differs from biases like confirmation bias and anchoring.

## A note on limits

Spotting distortions is a skill, and like any skill it's clumsy before it's automatic. Expect to catch them hours late at first, then minutes, then as they form. That progression is the whole point of daily practice.

This is also self-help, not treatment. CBT delivered by a trained therapist has decades of trial evidence behind it for depression and anxiety; reading a list of distortions is a smaller thing. If your mood is severe, persistent, or getting worse, work with a professional. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.

# How to Write a CBT Thought Record

> A step-by-step guide to the CBT thought record: the five columns, a worked example, and the four mistakes that make a thought record useless.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html
- Published: 2026-08-19
- Updated: 2026-11-03
- Reading time: 7 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** A thought record has five columns: the situation, the automatic thought, the emotion, the distortion, and a balanced thought. Writing the thought down turns it into something you can examine. Two or three records a week, each under five minutes, is enough. The aim is accuracy, not positivity.

A thought record is the exercise a CBT therapist will hand you in roughly week two. It looks like homework and it is, but the mechanism is worth understanding: writing the thought down moves it from something you're inside of to something you're looking at.

Classic versions have seven columns. Five is enough to get the effect, and five is short enough that you'll actually finish one at 11pm.

## Column 1 — The situation

What happened, in the register of a security camera. Who, what, where, when. No interpretation, no adjectives that do the judging for you.

> **Write:** "2:40pm, team standup. I gave the update on the migration. Priya asked when the timeline slipped."

Not "I got grilled in standup." That's already the distorted version, and if you start there the rest of the record just decorates it.

## Column 2 — The automatic thought

The sentence that ran through your head. Not a tidy summary of it — the actual words, including the ugly ones. Then rate how much you believe it, 0 to 100.

> **Write:** "They've worked out I'm not up to this job." *Belief: 85*

The belief rating matters more than it looks. It's the before-measurement, and without it you can't tell at the end whether anything moved.

If nothing comes, work backwards from the feeling: *what would I have to be thinking to feel this?* The thought is usually sitting right underneath, unexamined because it never had to defend itself.

## Column 3 — The emotion

One word, plus an intensity from 0 to 100. Shame. Anxiety. Anger. Humiliation.

> **Write:** "Shame — 75. Anxiety — 60."

One word, not a paragraph. "I felt like everyone could see through me" is another thought wearing a feeling's coat; put it in column two where it belongs. The discipline of a single word is what makes the rating meaningful.

## Column 4 — The distortion

Name the shape. Mind reading, in the example above — you've decided what the room concluded about you without anyone saying it. Often two or three overlap; write them all.

> **Write:** "Mind reading. Labelling ('not up to this job'). Mental filter — one question, ignoring the rest of the standup."

If the labels aren't familiar yet, the full list is here: [the 10 cognitive distortions, with examples](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html).

## Column 5 — The balanced thought

This is the column people get wrong, so it's worth being precise about the target. You are not writing the *opposite* of the automatic thought. You are writing what a fair witness — someone with all the information and no stake in your humiliation — would have said.

Three questions get you there:

- **What's the evidence for the thought?** Not feelings. Things that would hold up if someone else reviewed them.
- **What's the evidence against it?** Usually the harder list, because the mental filter has been discarding it all day.
- **What would I say to a friend who told me this?** The answer is nearly always kinder and more accurate at once, which tells you something.

> **Write:** "Priya asked one factual question about a date. She asks everyone factual questions — that's her job. Two people said the migration plan was clearer than the last one. I don't have evidence about what anyone concluded about me, only about what was asked." *Belief in original: 30. Shame: 35.*

Then re-rate. If the belief in the original thought dropped, the record worked. If it didn't move at all, the balanced thought is probably a slogan rather than an argument — go back and get more specific about the evidence.

## Four mistakes that make a thought record useless

### 1. Writing the interpretation in column one

"I got humiliated in standup" contaminates every column after it. Start with the camera footage.

### 2. Sanitising the automatic thought

If the thought was "I'm pathetic," write "I'm pathetic." The polite paraphrase is a different thought, and the one you actually believe goes unchallenged.

### 3. Reaching for positivity instead of accuracy

"I'm great at my job, actually" is a claim your brain can immediately refute, and it will. "One factual question is not a verdict" is small, defensible, and survives contact.

### 4. Only doing it when things are bad

Records written during a spike are the hardest and least accurate. A short one on an ordinary day builds the skill you'll need on the bad one.

## How often, and for how long

Two or three a week is plenty, and most take under five minutes once the format is familiar. The value compounds in a way a single record doesn't show: after a month you can look back and see that the same three distortions produce most of your bad afternoons. That's actionable in a way "I've been stressed lately" never is.

The goal isn't to keep writing records forever. It's to run the loop — trigger, emotion, distortion, reframe — quickly enough in your head that you stop needing the paper.

Each record is also a small vote against an old self-image. [Psycho-Cybernetics and CBT](https://behaviorized.net/articles/psycho-cybernetics-and-cbt.html) explains why that adds up.

## A note on limits

Thought records are a self-help tool with good evidence behind them as part of CBT, but they aren't treatment on their own, and they aren't the right first move for trauma or crisis. If your mood is severe, persistent, or worsening, work with a professional. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.

# Why Affirmations Don't Work — And What Does

> Positive affirmations can backfire for people with low self-esteem. Here's what the research found, why reframing works where repetition doesn't, and the order of operations that shifts a belief.

- Canonical URL: https://behaviorized.net/articles/affirmations-vs-reframing.html
- Published: 2026-08-19
- Updated: 2026-11-03
- Reading time: 6 min read
- Author: Hexp Studios, publisher of the Reframed app

> **In short:** Affirmations can backfire for people with low self-esteem: in Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009), repeating "I am a lovable person" made them feel worse. A claim your mind can refute gets refuted. Reframing works better: catch the thought, name the pattern, test it against evidence, and write the accurate version. Affirm it afterwards if you like.

The instruction is everywhere: say the good thing until you believe it. Write it on the mirror. Say it in the car. Eventually the repetition wins.

For some people it does help a little. For the people who reach for it hardest — the ones who already think poorly of themselves — the evidence suggests it can make things worse.

## What the research actually found

The best-known study is Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009), published in *Psychological Science*. Participants repeated the statement "I am a lovable person" and were then measured on mood and self-esteem.

People who already had high self-esteem felt slightly better. People with low self-esteem felt *worse* — measurably worse mood than a control group who repeated nothing at all. The paper's title says it plainly: positive self-statements are powerful for some, but risky for others.

The explanation the authors offer is straightforward once you've felt it. A statement far outside what you currently believe doesn't get accepted; it triggers a rebuttal. You say "I am a lovable person," and your mind — which has been keeping records — produces the counter-evidence. The affirmation is the prompt; the counter-argument is the response. You've just run a rehearsal of your own case against yourself.

It's a single line of research, not settled law, and later work has found affirmation-style exercises useful in other framings — particularly *values* affirmation, where you write about something that matters to you rather than asserting a trait you doubt. But the mechanism holds up as a warning: a claim your brain can refute will get refuted.

## The order of operations problem

Here's the structural issue. An affirmation is a new belief laid on top of an old one that is still running.

> **Still running:** "I don't follow through on anything."

> **Laid on top:** "I am disciplined and consistent."

Nothing has been removed. You've added a second, contradictory statement to a mind that already holds the first one with years of remembered evidence behind it. When the two collide, the one with the receipts wins.

Cognitive reframing reverses the order. You deal with the existing belief first — you catch it, name the pattern it follows, and test it against the evidence — and only then is there room for something else to land.

## What a reframe looks like next to an affirmation

The difference isn't tone. It's whether the sentence can be argued with.

> **Affirmation:** "I am confident and capable in every meeting."

Immediately refutable. Your brain has a specific meeting in mind already.

> **Reframe:** "I lost my thread for ten seconds and recovered. Two people followed up afterwards, which they don't do when something's unusable."

Nothing in that is cheerful, and that's why it works. It's specific, it's checkable, and there's no counter-argument available because it doesn't overclaim. It's the version a fair witness would give.

Do that a few dozen times and something more interesting happens: the evidence accumulates on the other side. You're no longer asserting a new identity, you're building a file for it — and the file is what eventually changes the verdict.

## So when are affirmations useful?

Last, not first — and only when the gap is small.

Once you've spent weeks catching "I don't follow through," naming it as overgeneralisation, and logging the twelve times you did follow through, "I finish what I start" stops being a claim your brain rejects. It's now a summary of a file you've actually built. Repeating it is consolidation rather than argument.

Two other things make affirmations land better, both supported by the research:

- **Aim at values, not traits.** "Doing careful work matters to me" is not refutable in the way "I am excellent at my job" is. Values affirmation is the version with the stronger evidence base.
- **Keep the distance short.** A statement one step ahead of where you are gets accepted. Ten steps ahead gets a rebuttal.

## The practical sequence

- **Catch the thought.** The actual sentence, in its actual words.
- **Name the pattern.** All-or-nothing, mind reading, labelling — see [the ten distortions](https://behaviorized.net/articles/cognitive-distortions.html).
- **Test it.** Evidence for, evidence against, what you'd say to a friend. The [thought record](https://behaviorized.net/articles/thought-record.html) is the formal version.
- **Write the accurate version.** Not the nice one. The one that survives scrutiny.
- **Then, if you like, the affirmation.** As a summary of what you've proved, not a substitute for proving it.

Repetition isn't the mechanism. Evidence is. Repetition just makes the verdict stick once you've won the case.

If you came to this through mindset books, [Psycho-Cybernetics and CBT](https://behaviorized.net/articles/psycho-cybernetics-and-cbt.html) covers how the self-image idea fits with this method.

## A note on limits

Reframing is a self-help technique drawn from CBT, not a treatment in itself. If low self-esteem is severe or long-standing, or your mood is getting worse, work with a professional. If you're in crisis, contact your local emergency service or a crisis line.
